name: California Bungalow

geography.hearth: Pasadena and Los Angeles, California, spreading through the Central Valley and the Southwest

lineage.note: The Southern Californian expression, and the one in which the style was invented before it was exported. The regional differences are all climatic: no snow load permits a lower pitch, no freeze permits single-wall construction, and a dry warm year permits rooms that are outdoors.

Shares the Californian stucco trade, the low-pitched tile or composition roof, and the pergola. Produces the common Los Angeles hybrid of a Craftsman body with stucco walls and a shaped parapet or tiled porch roof.

From 1915 onward the same builders and the same plaster crews shift toward the Spanish idiom; late California bungalows carry arched openings, red tile accents, and wrought iron while keeping the bungalow plan intact. This hybrid is what supplants the node rather than a separate style displacing it.

The gable-end truss displayed as a face, the projecting purlin, and the deep bracketed rake are more pronounced here than in the national type, because Californian builders learned them from the chalet pattern books that circulated on the West Coast in the 1880s and 1890s.

description.short: The Southern Californian bungalow in which the Craftsman grammar was first assembled, distinguished from the national type by lower pitches, deeper shading eaves, stucco and boulder masonry, and a set of genuinely outdoor rooms — sleeping porch, pergola, court — that only its climate permits.
description.long:
The California bungalow is the parent form pretending to be a child. The Craftsman style was assembled here, in Pasadena and Los Angeles between roughly 1903 and 1909, out of the chalet books, the British reform journals, the Japanese timber work at the expositions, and the local availability of redwood, arroyo boulders, and over-fired clinker brick from the Los Angeles yards. It then travelled east through Stickley's magazine and the plan-book trade and returned to the rest of the country in a form adapted for frost, snow load, and a heating bill. This node holds what was left behind in the adaptation, and almost all of it is climatic.

The climate does four things. It removes the snow load, which allows the roof to drop to three or four in twelve and to spread wide and flat, so that the Californian bungalow reads as a shelter placed on the ground rather than as a house with a lid. It makes shade rather than warmth the design problem, so eaves grow to three and four feet, porches deepen past eight, and pergolas, trellises, and vine-covered lattice extend the roof plane beyond the building. It removes the need for a continuous thermal envelope, which permits single-wall board-and-batten construction in the Central Valley and unheated rooms everywhere: the sleeping porch, screened and open on two or three sides, is a genuine room of the plan and not an afterthought. And it makes the year-round outdoor room possible, which produces the bungalow court — a row of small detached bungalows facing a shared landscaped walk rather than the street, of which Arthur and Alfred Heineman's Bowen Court in Pasadena, twenty-three units built 1910-1912, is the largest surviving example, and which remains one of the best pieces of low-rise dense housing ever built in America.

What produced it economically was the Southern California land boom that ran from about 1904 to 1913: the Pacific Electric interurban network opening subdivisions at a rate no other American city matched, a fifty-by-one-hundred-and-fifty-foot lot as the standard unit, and a house that could be built for fifteen hundred to three thousand dollars. Health migration supplied a large share of the buyers, and the sleeping porch is partly a tuberculosis prescription made architectural. The bungalow was marketed as a way of life more explicitly than any American house before it — informal, servantless, sunlit, out of doors — and the marketing was accurate, which is why the type survived the style.

The experience is of a building whose most important space is not enclosed. You arrive under a pergola or through a low masonry gate, cross a porch deep enough to be dim at midday, and the transition from outside to inside takes twenty feet and three changes of light. The masonry is deliberately rough — river boulders with mortar raked back, clinker brick warped and glazed by overfiring — set against woodwork that is machined flat and finished smooth, and the collision of the two textures is the whole aesthetic argument in one wall. The wood is redwood or Douglas fir, stained rather than painted, and in the surviving unmodernized examples it is very dark. Outside at the eave, the rafter tails are cut to a profile and the ends are sanded, which is the Japanese lesson: the end of a piece of wood is a face.

defining_characteristics: Very low roof pitch, 3:12 to 5:12, with eaves and rakes of 30 to 48 in shading the wall for most of the day
Porch of 8 ft or more depth, framed under the primary roof, with the roof plane frequently extended further by pergola, trellis, or beam extension
At least one genuinely outdoor or unheated room integral to the plan — sleeping porch, screened porch, or open court
Rustic local masonry — arroyo boulder, clinker brick, or cobble — at foundation, porch base, chimney, and site walls
Stucco, redwood shingle, or wide board-and-batten wall surfaces rather than the eastern type's clapboard
Exposed and shaped structural members: rafter tails cut to a profile, purlins projecting through the gable, beam ends sanded and finished
Single storey or single storey with one raised sleeping room; no full second floor
diagnostic_tells: Roof pitch visibly below 5:12 with an overhang deep enough to stand under
Arroyo boulder or clinker brick used raw against smooth machined woodwork on the same porch
A pergola, trellis, or extended open beam structure continuing the roof plane past the enclosed wall
Sleeping porch on the upper level, screened rather than glazed, often with its own small hipped roof
In the airplane subtype, a single room raised above the main roof with windows on all four sides and no dormer relationship to the roof below

distinguished_from.difference: The national plan-book type has steeper pitch (4:12-6:12), shallower eaves, clapboard or shingle rather than stucco, and no unheated rooms. It is a Californian design rebuilt for winter.

Mission Revival organizes the elevation around a shaped parapet, arcade, and red tile roof, and has no exposed timber. Where both appear, look at the gable: an exposed truss with projecting purlins is bungalow, a curvilinear parapet is Mission.

Spanish Colonial Revival turns the wall into a smooth plastic mass with deeply recessed openings and no eave; the bungalow keeps the wall thin and the eave deep. If the roof stops at the wall, it is Spanish; if the roof flies past it, it is bungalow.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The Craftsman datums with a shade override. Roof plane and eave depth are set first, by the sun angle and by the depth of shadow wanted on the wall, and the enclosed volume is then fitted beneath. This inverts the usual sequence — the roof is designed before the plan — and is why the type tolerates such wide dimensional variation without losing coherence.
typical_ratios: Eave and rake overhang 30 to 48 in
Ceiling 8 ft 6 in to 9 ft 6 in — taller than the eastern type, for stack ventilation
Body width 24 to 30 ft; depth 36 to 50 ft
Masonry porch base 24 to 36 in wide, carrying a tapered post no more than half its width
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Grouped openings of two to four sash between exposed posts, with the porch reading as one very wide bay occupying the whole street elevation.

massing_affinities.note: Invented in and largely confined to California and the Central Valley; the raised room is a sleeping porch catching the evening breeze.
The bungalow court reads as a courtyard-U at site scale, with the units detached rather than continuous.

constraints.statement: This assembly — 3:12 to 5:12 pitch, unlined deep eaves, single-wall or minimally insulated walls, unheated rooms — is native to IECC zones 2B, 3B and 3C only. In zones 5 and above the pitch must rise to 4:12-6:12, the eave shorten to 24-36 in, and the outdoor rooms be glazed, at which point the node becomes craftsman-bungalow.

test.note: Tests the pitch range this node is native to. The IECC-zone gating and the zone-5-and-above conversion to craftsman-bungalow are conditional/descriptive rather than a bound on this node's own values, and there is no climate-zone vocabulary variable -- both stay prose.

constraints.statement: Eave and rake overhang not less than 30 in; porch depth not less than 8 ft clear.

test.note: Tests the eave/rake overhang. Porch depth (not less than 8 ft, expressible via gallery_depth_ft) is a second independent numeric clause and is left as prose rather than combined into this test.

constraints.statement: Masonry at porch base, chimney, and foundation must be a locally rough material laid with raked joints; smooth-faced manufactured veneer with returns of less than 24 in is forbidden.
Rafter tails, purlin ends, and beam ends must be cut to a declared profile and finished on the end grain; square sawn-off ends are permitted only on secondary structures.
At least one unheated or open room — sleeping porch, screened porch, pergola-covered terrace of not less than 80 sq ft — must be present in the plan.

exemplars.name: Bowen Court
exemplars.note: Arthur and Alfred Heineman, 1910-1912. Twenty-three bungalows in an L about a shared garden walk; one of the largest bungalow courts in Southern California.
exemplars.why: The type specimen for the bungalow COURT, which is the one plan type this node has that the national type does not: the Pasadena bungalow-courts nomination calls it 'the most well known extant bungalow court in Pasadena, and perhaps in the larger Los Angeles region as well' and 'one of the two oldest to survive', and Wikipedia 'one of the largest bungalow courts in southern California'. The node's own long description calls its twenty-three units about a shared walk the largest surviving example; no source the record carries says largest, so that superlative is this project's and not the register's.

exemplars.name: Bungalow Heaven Landmark District
exemplars.note: More than 800 bungalows, c. 1900-1930, designated 1989 — the Californian type at street scale rather than at exhibition scale.
exemplars.why: The type at street scale rather than at exhibition scale -- the California Office of Historic Preservation counts '522 contributing and 164 non-contributing buildings' and calls it 'the largest intact grouping of working class housing constructed during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries reflecting the influences of the Arts and Crafts movement in Pasadena'; a landmark district in 1989 and on the National Register in 2008 -- and it is a district, so it can stand for a neighbourhood's practice and not for a building's rule. The note's 'more than 800' is the Wikipedia page this record cites and does not quote; the register's own count is the one above.

exemplars.name: Gamble House
exemplars.note: Greene and Greene. Included as the type's apotheosis and its explicit outlier: a bungalow grammar executed at ten times the normal budget, with the sleeping porches, terraces, and boulder masonry of the modest type at full scale.
exemplars.why: The building the type is known by and its explicit outlier, on the HABS survey's own significance line calling it 'California Bungalow style ... one of the finest examples of the American Craftsman Movement' -- the node's own exemplar note already says it is a bungalow grammar at ten times the budget.

exemplars.name: Lanterman House
exemplars.note: Arthur L. Haley, 1915. A reinforced-concrete bungalow built as a U about a patio, ringed by a trellised terrace on concrete columns -- the node's outdoor rooms built as the whole plan rather than added to one face.
exemplars.why: A documented type specimen whose National Register nomination lists it for exactly this node's own climatic argument -- 'architecture meant to take advantage of the micro-climate for optimum air circulation and sun exposure in this inland valley area' -- so the reason it is on the register is the reason the node exists.

exemplars.name: Major Harry E. Kunkel House
exemplars.location: 1542 North McCadden Place, Los Angeles, California
exemplars.note: Architect unknown, 1910. A plain Los Angeles bungalow the Historic American Buildings Survey measured: 31 x 52 ft, one storey, no chimney. The ordinary article, in the hearth, with a figure attached.
exemplars.why: Plain, surveyed and useful to measure rather than to admire: HABS recorded it (CA-2969) and no register was found that lists it, which is the definition of this standing and the judgment is the Survey's.

exemplars.name: Ivan Carter McIndoo House
exemplars.note: Architect unknown, ca. 1913, moved from 410 North Van Ness Avenue about 1992. A Central Valley bungalow at the larger 'bungaloid' scale, with a full HABS Part II description of its walls, eaves and openings.
exemplars.why: A surveyed plain example in the Central Valley reach this node's own long description names, carried for its measurable Part II description rather than for its quality; the year is null because the survey itself says only 'ca. 1913'.

sources: Edward R. Bosley, Greene and Greene (2000)
Stefanos Polyzoides, Roger Sherwood and James Tice, Courtyard Housing in Los Angeles (1982)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)

proportion_packs.note: The branch that designs the roof before the plan, which its own record calls out as inverting the usual sequence. Two of the pack's figures sit at the top of their bands here for stated reasons rather than by preference: the eave at 30-48 in, because its depth is set by the shadow wanted on the wall, and the ceiling at 8 ft 6 in to 9 ft 6 in for stack ventilation. Read the eave rule and the daylight rule together on this node -- a 48 in overhang buys glazing that a 24 in one does not, and this is the node where that trade was made deliberately.

Inherited from the parent craftsman style (regional_of, weight 1) with the same datum-band and roof-dominance logic, and especially apt here: this node's own porch_depth figure (8-12 ft clear) sits almost exactly on this pack's own porch_depth rule ('eight feet... close to a hard number rather than a soft one... the band in which a porch is both usable and survivable for the rooms behind'), and the pack's roof_form ratio (dominant roof covers at least half to 0.85 of the elevation) matches this variant's even lower 3:12-5:12 pitch and 30-48 in eaves better than it matches the national type's.

Carried from the parent style: the same catalog carpentry logic, built here in redwood and Douglas fir rather than eastern species, which the pack itself does not distinguish by wood type and does not need to.

Bound narrowly for one mechanism: this pack's daylight-strategy conflict entry states plainly that 'an eight-foot porch across a south front costs the rooms behind it about four feet of usable depth' and that the historic answer was to raise the storey to buy the loss back -- which is exactly this variant's own defining move (ceilings 8 ft 6 in to 9 ft 6 in, 'taller than the eastern type, for stack ventilation,' per its own typical_ratios) and exactly why its sleeping porches and courts are genuinely unheated rooms rather than mere ornament. Not bound for room proportion generally: this is an architect- and pattern-book-derived type, not a span/hearth-constrained folk one, and its rooms are sized by the plan-book programme, which the node's own text describes directly.

declined_packs.reason: A rule for graduating a stack of storeys has no stack to graduate. This node's own record makes a single storey (or one and a half) definitional, so `height_proportion` arriving as a second-to-first-storey ratio dimensions a floor the house does not have.
declined_packs.quote: Single storey or single storey with one raised sleeping room; no full second floor
declined_packs.note: Declined, not merely unendorsed: the pack reached this node through the cascade and nobody had ever judged it. `--impact` first — on ranch-style the pack governs one interior slot and nothing is left undimensioned; on craftsman-bungalow it governs none.

declined_packs.reason: The pack's notes state exactly what it emits: given a room, three ceiling heights by the harmonic, geometric and arithmetic means of its plan dimensions, 19 ft 2 in to 20 ft 0 in for a 16 x 24 room. The node states its own ceiling as a fixed 8 ft 6 in to 9 ft 6 in band and names a non-proportional cause for it -- stack ventilation, and being taller than the eastern type -- and a fixed band cannot be a mean of the room's plan dimensions, because a mean scales with the room and this does not. The node's own proportion_packs note says the same thing one layer out, that its rooms are sized by the plan-book programme and that it is not bound for room proportion generally. The derivation the pack offers for ceiling_height_rule is one this record has already answered differently, in its own words.
declined_packs.quote: Ceiling 8 ft 6 in to 9 ft 6 in — taller than the eastern type, for stack ventilation
declined_packs.note: Governs 0 slots on this node: declining changes no dimension and nothing loses all dimensioning. No live gate -- endorsing or declining changes only the meter and the judged count.
